title: Reading a basis-set heat map and a conformer: what the overlap matrix and a projected geometry can and cannot tell
summary: A heat map of orbital overlaps shows how atomic orbitals of a molecule talk to each other in a minimal basis, and a pair of projections shows a sampled molecular conformer. Both are inputs to quantum chemistry, not results, and both come with caveats stated in their titles.

media.alt: Square heat map titled absolute overlap for malonaldehyde in a minimal basis, 29 atomic orbitals, geometry from a force-field embedding and not optimized quantum-chemically. Rows and columns are labelled by atom and orbital (O0:1s, O0:2px and so on). A bright yellow diagonal runs from top left to bottom right; off-diagonal cells are mostly dark purple with small patches of teal and green near each atom's own orbitals and between neighbouring atoms.

read_the_figure.question: Which orbitals overlap appreciably, and is the geometry one you can trust for a quantum calculation?
read_the_figure.axes: Overlap map: both axes list the 29 atomic orbitals grouped by atom (every other label printed); colour is the absolute value of the overlap |S_pq| from 0 (dark purple) to 1 (yellow). Geometry plots: x against y (left) and x against z (right) in angstrom, atoms as dots with labels, hydrogens hidden.
look_at: The diagonal is exactly 1: every orbital overlaps itself fully because the basis functions are normalized.

Blocks near the diagonal: orbitals on the same atom (1s with 2s, for example) overlap a little; the 2p functions of one atom do not overlap each other (they are orthogonal), which shows as dark off-diagonal cells inside a block.
Teal and green patches off the diagonal block: neighbouring bonded atoms; the largest values, around 0.5 to 0.6, link a carbon 2s with a hydrogen 1s.
Title caveats: minimal basis (STO-3G, 29 functions) and a geometry that came from a force-field embedding and is not quantum-optimized, so the numbers describe that geometry only.

Geometry figure: a chain of carbons (dark) and two oxygens (orange) projected onto two planes; positions that overlap in one projection are separated in the other (C9 and C10 in x-y, C7 and C8 in x-z).
The label 'sampled MMFF94 candidate' says this is one conformer drawn from a force-field search, not an energy minimum.
read_the_figure.proves: The overlap matrix is a property of the basis and the geometry alone; it does not contain any electronic-structure result. It shows how far from orthogonal the basis is, which matters for the numerical stability of the eigenproblem. The geometry shows what structure the later calculation would start from.
if_wrong: An overlap diagonal different from 1: the basis is not normalized.
Off-diagonal elements of magnitude near 1 between different functions: nearly linear dependence, which makes the eigenproblem ill-conditioned.
Interpreting a force-field geometry as a quantum-chemical minimum: bond lengths and angles may differ from optimized ones.
Reading distances from one projection: a 2D projection hides the third coordinate.
must_check: That the basis set and the number of functions are stated.
That the geometry's origin (force field or optimized) is in the title.
That the colour scale is given and the quantity is the absolute value.
That both projections of a 3D structure are shown and the axes carry units.

terms.meaning: The set of functions in which the molecular orbitals are expanded.
The matrix of integrals of products of basis functions; the identity if the basis is orthonormal.
A minimal basis in which each atomic orbital is fitted by three Gaussians.
One of the three-dimensional arrangements of a flexible molecule obtained by rotating bonds.
A standard molecular-mechanics force field used to generate and rank conformers cheaply.

remember: S is symmetric, has unit diagonal for normalized functions and is positive definite.
Orbitals of one atom with different angular character are orthogonal: S = 0 between 2px and 2py of the same atom.
The Roothaan equations are a generalized eigenproblem F C = S C epsilon.
A minimal basis for C3H4O2 has 29 functions: 5 for each heavy atom and 1 for each hydrogen.
A force-field geometry is a starting point; its energies and distances are not quantum results.

steps.title: The overlap of two normalized s Gaussians
steps.note: The off-diagonal numbers shrink exponentially with distance: bonded neighbours overlap strongly, distant atoms hardly at all, which is why the matrix is nearly block-diagonal.

steps.title: Why the overlap enters the eigenproblem
steps.note: The basis is not orthogonal, so the energy equations carry S. Orthogonalizing by S to the power minus one half turns them into an ordinary eigenproblem; a nearly singular S would amplify numerical errors.

steps.title: Counting basis functions
steps.note: Carbon and oxygen each carry 1s, 2s, 2px, 2py, 2pz in STO-3G; hydrogen only 1s. The figure's 29 follows from the formula of malonaldehyde, C3H4O2.

steps.title: A bond length from coordinates
steps.note: Using both projections of the geometry figure (read by eye), the C3-C4 distance is about 1.49 angstrom, typical of a single carbon-carbon bond. A single projection would give only the in-plane part.

worked.title: Overlap of two 1s Gaussians at a bond distance
worked.problem: Two normalized s Gaussians with exponent 0.3 (atomic units) are 2 bohr apart. Compute S, and compare with the same exponent at 4 bohr.
worked.answer: 0.55 at 2 bohr and 0.09 at 4 bohr: doubling the distance cuts the overlap by a factor of six, hence the dark off-diagonal regions.

The title says the geometry was not optimized quantum-chemically. List two consequences for numbers derived from this matrix.

create: Compute the eigenvalues of the 29 by 29 overlap matrix and say what the smallest one would tell you.
Add bond lengths printed next to each bond in the geometry figure.

checks.answer: Each basis function is normalized, so its overlap with itself is one.

checks.q: How many basis functions has water in STO-3G?
Why does the overlap decrease with distance?
checks.answer: Products of Gaussians centred far apart are small everywhere, giving an exponentially small integral.

checks.q: A colleague says the heat map shows the molecule's bonding. True?
checks.answer: No: S depends only on the basis and geometry. Bonding appears in the density matrix and energies, not here.

checks.q: Design a heat map that shows chemical bonding rather than basis overlap.
checks.answer: Plot the bond order (Mayer or Wiberg) between atom pairs from the converged density matrix.
